title: The Holy Roman Empire
description: An illustrated map of the Holy Roman Empire, from Charlemagne’s crowning in 800 and Otto I in 962 through Canossa, Barbarossa and the Lombard League, Frederick II, Charles IV and the Golden Bull, the Council of Constance, the Habsburgs, Luther at Worms, the Thirty Years’ War, Westphalia and the Diet at Regensburg to Austerlitz and the end in 1806.
mapLabel: Illustrated map of the Holy Roman Empire, 800 to 1806
note: Based mainly on the chronicles of the period (Liudprand of Cremona, Lampert of Hersfeld, Otto of Freising, Matthew Paris), on the imperial charters and the Golden Bull, and on modern histories; each chapter says which it follows. Native names are Latin, the empire’s common language of record. Numbers for armies and deaths are given as the sources give them and are often disputed. The map is stylised and not to scale; coasts are drawn as they are today. Powers areas are loose and show the empire’s core, not its many frontiers.

steps.title: Charlemagne is crowned emperor
steps.text: Charlemagne, king of the Franks, was crowned emperor by Pope Leo III in St Peter’s, Rome, on Christmas Day 800. He had conquered Saxony and northern Italy and ruled from Aachen. His court revived learning. The coronation revived the Roman imperial title in the West. His empire split among his grandsons in 843.
steps.today: Today: Vatican City, Rome; Aachen’s cathedral holds his throne.

steps.title: Otto I and the new empire
steps.text: Otto I, king of the Germans, crushed the Magyars at the Lechfeld in 955 and was crowned emperor in Rome by Pope John XII on 2 February 962. The German kings who followed kept the title until 1806. The name “Holy Roman Empire” only came into use in the 13th century, after the empire’s long struggle with the popes.
steps.today: Today: Magdeburg, Germany, where Otto lies buried in the cathedral.

steps.title: Henry IV at Canossa
steps.text: Pope Gregory VII and King Henry IV quarrelled over who should appoint bishops, the Investiture Controversy. Excommunicated, and facing rebel princes, Henry crossed the Alps in midwinter and, chroniclers say, stood three days outside Canossa Castle in the snow until the pope forgave him in January 1077. He later returned and drove Gregory out of Rome.
steps.today: Today: Canossa, Emilia-Romagna, Italy; only ruins remain of the castle.

steps.title: Barbarossa and the Lombard League
steps.text: Frederick I Barbarossa (“Red Beard”) crossed the Alps six times to claim imperial rights over the rich cities of northern Italy. They formed the Lombard League with the pope, and at Legnano their militia beat his army. A treaty at Constance in 1183 left them self-governing under the emperor. He drowned in a river in Anatolia on crusade in 1190.

steps.title: Frederick II, the wonder of the world
steps.text: Frederick II grew up in Palermo, where Normans, Greeks and Arabs mixed. Crowned emperor in 1220, he regained Jerusalem by treaty in 1229 while under excommunication. He wrote a book on falconry and founded a university at Naples. Chroniclers called him stupor mundi, “wonder of the world”. After he died in 1250 imperial power in Italy collapsed.
steps.today: Today: Palermo, Sicily; Frederick is buried in the cathedral.

steps.title: Charles IV and the Golden Bull
steps.text: Charles IV, king of Bohemia, made Prague his capital and founded its university in 1348. His Golden Bull of 1356, issued at Nuremberg and Metz, named seven electors, three archbishops and four secular princes, who chose the king of the Romans. It fixed the rules for the next four centuries and strengthened the princes against the emperor.
steps.today: Today: Prague, Czechia; the Charles Bridge and the university bear his name.

steps.title: The Council of Constance
steps.text: King Sigismund called the Council of Constance to end the Western Schism, when three men claimed to be pope. It deposed or accepted the resignation of all three and elected Martin V. Jan Hus, a Czech preacher, came under a safe-conduct but was condemned and burned in July 1415. His followers began the Hussite Wars.
steps.today: Today: Konstanz, Germany, on Lake Constance; a statue of Hus stands in Prague.

steps.title: The Habsburgs and Vienna
steps.text: After 1438 the crown stayed almost always with the House of Habsburg, based in Vienna. Maximilian I married Mary of Burgundy in 1477, winning the Netherlands, and arranged marriages that later brought Spain to his grandson. A Latin saying runs: “Let others wage war; you, happy Austria, marry.” Maximilian reformed imperial courts and taxes.
steps.today: Today: Vienna, Austria; the Hofburg was the Habsburgs’ palace.

steps.title: Luther at the Diet of Worms
steps.text: Martin Luther, a monk and professor at Wittenberg, had attacked the sale of indulgences in 1517. Summoned to the Diet of Worms, he refused to retract before Emperor Charles V. The words “Here I stand” are often credited to him but are not certain. Charles outlawed him. Printing spread Luther’s writings and his German Bible, and the Reformation grew.
steps.today: Today: Worms, Germany; a Luther memorial stands in the city.

steps.title: The Thirty Years’ War
steps.text: In May 1618 Protestant nobles threw two imperial officials out of a window of Prague Castle. The war that followed drew in Sweden, France and Spain and ravaged the German lands. Fighting, famine and plague killed many; some estimates say a fifth or more of the population in the empire, but figures are disputed.
steps.today: Today: Prague Castle, Czechia; the window is among its tourist sights.

steps.title: The Peace of Westphalia
steps.text: Talks at Münster and Osnabrück ended the Thirty Years’ War in 1648. Lutherans, Catholics and Calvinists were all recognised. The princes gained the right to make their own alliances, so the emperor’s real power shrank. The Swiss Confederation and the Dutch Republic were recognised as independent. Historians still debate how far Westphalia made the modern state system.
steps.today: Today: Münster, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany; the Peace Hall of its town hall survives.

steps.title: The Diet at Regensburg
steps.text: After 1663 the imperial Diet (Reichstag) sat permanently at Regensburg, with delegates from hundreds of states, bishoprics and free cities. In 1803 it redrew the map, ending most church lands and many small states. Voltaire joked that the empire was neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire. Its law courts still worked.
steps.today: Today: Regensburg, Bavaria, Germany; the old town hall is a museum.

steps.title: Austerlitz
steps.text: Napoleon beat the armies of Austria and Russia at Austerlitz on 2 December 1805, often called the battle of the three emperors. Austria made peace at Pressburg. In July 1806 sixteen German states left the empire to join Napoleon’s Confederation of the Rhine. Napoleon then announced that he no longer recognised the empire.
steps.today: Today: Slavkov u Brna, Czechia, east of Brno.

steps.title: The empire is dissolved
steps.text: On 6 August 1806 Francis II declared that he no longer held the imperial crown and released the empire’s states from their duty to him. He had styled himself Emperor of Austria since 1804. The Holy Roman Empire, which had lasted since 962, had ended. Its Imperial Crown is now kept in Vienna.
steps.today: Today: Vienna; the Imperial Crown is in the Hofburg treasury.

items.name: Holy Roman Empire

facts.Capital: None fixed; the court moved, and Prague and Vienna were its chief seats
facts.Language: Latin for law and church; German in everyday use
facts.Government: An elected king and emperor, with princes, bishops and free cities
facts.Began: 962 with Otto I, or 800 with Charlemagne as its prologue
facts.Ended: 6 August 1806, when Francis II laid down the crown
facts.Today: Germany, Austria, Czechia, Switzerland, Belgium, the Netherlands and northern Italy

items.role: The Holy Roman Empire: a loose union of German, Bohemian, Burgundian and Italian lands under an elected emperor, from Otto I in 962 to Francis II in 1806, with Charlemagne’s empire as its prologue.

items.name: Charlemagne
items.text: Charlemagne became king of the Franks in 768 and doubled his realm by conquest. He fought the Saxons for thirty years and took the Lombard kingdom in Italy. He gathered scholars at Aachen, including Alcuin, and standardised weights and the coinage. His coronation as emperor in 800 set the pattern for later rulers.

items.name: Otto I
items.text: Otto, son of Henry the Fowler, put down rebel dukes and gave church lands and bishops duties as royal officials. After the Lechfeld victory he was hailed “the Great”. Crowned emperor in 962, he made Magdeburg an archbishopric and relied on bishops and abbots as royal officials. He is buried at Magdeburg.

items.name: Frederick II
items.text: Frederick, grandson of Barbarossa, was king of Sicily from infancy and emperor from 1220. He spoke several languages, patronised poets and scientists and issued the Constitutions of Melfi in 1231, a law code for Sicily. He fought the popes for decades. They called him the Antichrist, and admirers called him stupor mundi.

items.name: Charles IV
items.text: Charles, born Wenceslas in Prague, became king of Bohemia and, in 1355, emperor. A scholar who wrote his own life story, he founded the first university in central Europe at Prague, built Charles Bridge and Karlštejn Castle, and secured peace through the Golden Bull. He is regarded as the father of the Czech lands.

items.name: Martin Luther
items.text: Luther, an Augustinian friar and professor at Wittenberg, attacked the sale of indulgences in 1517. Refusing to recant at Worms, he was sheltered in the Wartburg, where he translated the New Testament into German. His writings, spread by printing, split western Christianity. His followers took the name Lutherans, though he never wanted a new church.

items.name: Francis II
items.text: Francis, born in Florence, became emperor in 1792, in the middle of war with revolutionary France. After defeat at Austerlitz he gave up the imperial crown in 1806, keeping the title Emperor Francis I of Austria. After 1815 he worked with his minister Metternich to restore the old order. He died in 1835, after forty-three years on the throne.
